aions_core/agi_existing_models.py: This file acts as a hub that discovers and manages language models already installed on the computer—specifically Mistral-7B, Phi-3 (modified for Korean), and Bielik. It loads each model only when needed, using either llama.cpp for compressed formats or the transformers library for PyTorch models, keeping only one model in memory at a time to save RAM. The file includes Korean syllable compression that reduces text size using patterns, and chunk loading from CBMS (code book memory system) JSON and binary files. When you ask it a question, it picks the best model based on what you're asking about, retrieves relevant chunks from memory, and generates an answer. An ensemble version runs multiple models and picks the best response. The system tracks how fast each query runs and what chunks were used.
aions_core/aions_crla_reformed.py: This file combines cleaned seed data from reformed CBMS with a tournament system (CRLA) for picking the best answer. When you ask a question, it first tries to answer directly from stored facts. If there's no direct answer and the memory system retrieves too many chunks (panic threshold), it generates multiple candidate answers, scores each one using a metric formula, runs them through a tournament, and picks the winner. The winning answer gets saved as a derivation with timestamp and trace showing which candidates were considered. High-confidence direct answers are saved as facts. The system detects when it's overwhelmed with too much information (panic) and switches strategies. The file imports existing modules for memory, CBMS integration, and CRLA scoring, testing the complete workflow.
aions_core/aions_monitoring_dashboard.py: This file is a production-ready monitoring system that watches over an AIONS installation and makes sure everything works. It runs a comprehensive test suite across core, vector search, and hybrid retrieval components, checking that each one responds correctly. The monitoring system tracks how fast queries run, measures success rates, and logs errors. A health check verifies each component is operational. Performance benchmarking runs queries repeatedly and calculates percentiles (95th, 99th) to understand response time distribution. All test results, performance metrics, and error logs get saved to files with timestamps. The system generates a human-readable report showing which components are working, what tests passed or failed, and how the system is performing overall, outputting everything as JSON and text summaries.
aions_core/aions_vector_enhancement.py: This file adds semantic search using LanceDB, a vector database that finds information by meaning rather than exact words. It connects to an existing LanceDB instance used by Kiro (another system in the environment), specifically looking for a table containing knowledge documents. When you search, it scans the database and returns relevant results with similarity scores. The file discovers what tables exist and connects to the main knowledge table. It provides statistics about the database like how many rows are stored. Without the embedding model loaded separately, it does basic limit-scanned retrieval instead of true semantic search, so full text-to-vector search requires additional setup. The connection shows table names and row counts proving it's communicating with the vector database.
aions_core/tools/symbolic_probe.py: This file demonstrates how natural language gets translated into symbolic codes for memory lookups in CBMS. It dynamically loads three helper modules (Esperanto bridge, codebook engine, symbolic index) from the server directory. The demo takes plain-language Polish queries and converts each one to Esperanto as an intermediate step, then encodes the Esperanto into CBMS codes using a codebook. These codes represent concepts in machine-readable way. It then searches the symbolic index for chunks matching those codes and shows which chunk IDs scored highest. The workflow proves that questions like 'I went to the store today' and 'Explain Korean-CBMS segmentation' can be reduced to symbolic patterns that match stored information blocks without needing vector embeddings.
aions_core/tools/test_guardrail.py: This file tests whether the system correctly refuses nonsensical queries and accepts valid ones. It sends HTTP requests to a running server (port 8080) with two test cases: gibberish text that should be rejected, and a legitimate Polish question that should get answered. For each test, it prints the HTTP response status and full JSON reply showing what the server decided. The test demonstrates the guardrail policy—a protective layer that filters out meaningless input to prevent wasting computation on garbage. If the server responds successfully to the good query and refuses the bad one, the guardrail is working. The test can run locally against any AIONS server on 127.0.0.1, validating that input filtering is operational.
control_plane/agents/__init__.py: This docstring-only file explains the agent engine design philosophy: agents are declarations that describe roles within CBMS (code book memory system), not separate execution code. Each agent is a folder containing an agent.json configuration file declaring what it does. The system auto-discovers agents by scanning the agents_lib directory—when you drop a new agent folder there, it's automatically available without touching core code. An agent is essentially a read-only view into the existing skill registry and execution gate with a risk cap. Agents own no logic; they describe how to combine existing skills safely. This plug-and-play architecture means adding new agent roles is configuration, not programming, keeping the system modular and preventing code churn.
control_plane/models.py: This file defines data structures that represent plans and their execution in a control system. A PlanStep contains a task description, the name of the tool that should run it, and arguments for that tool. A Plan collects multiple steps along with an overall intent statement and CBMS context chunks that inform the plan. ExecutionResult records what happened when one step ran: its status, output, error message if it failed, and how long it took in milliseconds. ExecutionState tracks overall progress: which plan is running, what status it's in, which step is currently executing, and the results from all steps so far. Helper functions generate unique IDs for plans and steps using UUID to ensure no collisions.
control_plane/operator/loop.py: This is the operator automation loop that runs continuously to detect and fix system problems. It follows a five-phase cycle: observe (collect system stats), diagnose (identify issues), act (take corrective steps), verify (confirm issues are resolved), and learn (save incident record). The observe phase gathers memory usage, disk usage, failed services, and error log counts using shell skills. Diagnose applies threshold rules—if disk is over 90%, if a service failed, if load average is too high, or if error counts spike. Act recommends fixes or takes automatic action like restarting a service with safeguards like restart cooldowns. Verify re-observes to check whether the fix worked. Learn saves incident records to JSON log, optionally adding LLM commentary in Polish when actions escalate to human review.
scripts/chatgpt_ultimate.py: This script extracts everything stored in ChatGPT Desktop's local cache files and produces a clean inventory. It reads raw LevelDB text dumps and parses them with regex patterns to find user emails, display names, user IDs, message counts, conversation titles, custom GPTs the user created, draft messages, and model access information like GPT-5 availability. Some data is stored as spaced-out text (each letter separated by spaces), so the script reconstructs normal words. It generates two output files: a JSON file with all extracted data organized by category, and a markdown report showing conversation history, model access levels, and custom GPT list. The script handles encoding issues and malformed data gracefully, keeping everything readable.
scripts/demo_papiery.py: This demo script shows how to use CBMS blocks to manage personal tasks and reminders like a digital secretary. It loads the skill registry which discovers all available CBMS blocks, then adds sample papers (tasks) with titles, deadlines, and priority levels. The secretary then lists all stored papers, finds papers due soon (within 7 days), and sends a system notification reminding the user of urgent items. The script also searches for papers matching a keyword. Finally, it demonstrates how the skill registry's search function picks the right CBMS block for a question by returning the best match. All task data lives in local JSON files within your CBMS directory, not in a remote database. The demo proves CBMS blocks can replace apps for task management.
scripts/test_llm_adapter.py: This test verifies that the Polish language model (Bielik via Ollama) answers correctly and uses injected context. It defines test questions with expected keywords that prove context was used: 'Who am I?' should mention the operator's name from operator_profile.json, and 'What is CBMS?' should reference the chunked memory system with words like 'chunks' or 'memory'. The test runs each question, checks if the response contains Polish language indicators (Polish characters and common words), then checks if expected context keywords appear. If the model responds in Polish AND uses provided context, the test passes. The script handles Ollama server availability gracefully, reporting whether the model endpoint is reachable and which models are loaded.
scripts/validate_aions_tools.py: This script quickly validates that MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool functions work after code changes. It imports tool implementations from the server module and runs quick tests: search for Python files, search in specific folders, check system health, search the code book memory, retrieve facts from long-term memory, check git status, list WSL distributions, list Docker containers, check project scan status, check conversation status, list MCP servers, and check thinking process status. Each tool should return a response with status='ok' or status='completed'. The script counts how many tests passed and reports totals. This is a smoke test confirming the server can execute its tools—useful after changes to ensure nothing broke.
server/app.py: This is the main REST API server that manages a knowledge base with sessions, search, and document storage. Built with FastAPI, it listens for HTTP requests to add documents to a session, search for relevant documents, and manage sessions. Sessions are like workspaces—each one has its own collection of documents. The API provides endpoints to add context batches (text plus metadata), search using a query with optional filters, list all sessions with statistics, get details about one session, dump all documents from a session, prune expired documents, and view a dashboard summary. The server connects to a vector store (ChromaDB) that actually holds the data. CORS is enabled so clients from any origin can connect. Optional control plane routes can be added if available.
server/store_http.py: This file implements the vector storage backend using ChromaDB with two connection modes: HTTP (connecting to a remote server) or embedded (local storage). It tries first to connect via HTTP to a ChromaDB server on 127.0.0.1:8000, falling back to embedded mode if the server is down. Collections are created per session, keeping documents and their metadata organized. When you search, it converts Chroma's distance scores to similarity scores (0 to 1) accounting for the actual distance metric used (L2, cosine, inner product). It handles keyword boosting to increase scores for documents matching all query words. The store tracks which mode it's using and logs degraded-to-embedded failures to a runtime log. It can reconnect to HTTP mode later if the server comes back online.
